title: The Galois closure of ℚ(⁴√2): why it is ℚ(⁴√2, i) of degree 8
content: The docstring frames the entry against the parent fourth-root-2-irrational ([ℚ(⁴√2):ℚ] = 4 via Eisenstein on X⁴ − 2) and its open question OQ-01: find the Galois closure. Because X⁴ − 2 has the non-real roots ±i·⁴√2, the field ℚ(⁴√2) — which contains only the real root — is not normal; its Galois closure is the splitting field ℚ(⁴√2, i). The plan is a quadratic tower ℚ ⊂ ℚ(⁴√2) ⊂ ℚ(⁴√2, i) with steps of degree 4 and 2, giving degree 8, the strict second step being the crux i ∉ ℚ(⁴√2).
mathContext: ℚ(⁴√2, i) is the classic first example of a non-normal radical extension with non-abelian Galois group D₄.
prerequisites: The tower law for field degrees

title: The degree-4 base field ℚ(⁴√2) inside ℂ
content: The parent works with the real number ⁴√2 = √√2, but the Galois closure needs i, so everything moves into ℂ. Here a = (⁴√2 : ℂ) is the real root coerced to ℂ; a_pow_four lifts (⁴√2)⁴ = 2 across the coercion, and a_im records that a is real (Im a = 0). Since X⁴ − 2 is irreducible over ℚ (the parent's Eisenstein + Gauss result) and a is a root of the monic X⁴ − 2, minpoly_a gives minpoly ℚ a = X⁴ − 2 and finrank_adjoin_a gives [ℚ(⁴√2):ℚ] = 4 via IntermediateField.adjoin.finrank.
mathContext: The bottom step of the tower, transported from the parent's real computation to the complex embedding.
relatedConcepts: complex embedding of a real field

title: Realizing ℝ as an intermediate field — the crux i ∉ ℚ(⁴√2)
content: The whole obstruction to normality is that ℚ(⁴√2) lives inside ℝ and misses i. To make this a usable field-theoretic bound, realSubfield is the subfield of ℂ with zero imaginary part (closure under +, ×, −, ⁻¹ each following from Complex.mul_im / add_im / neg_im / inv_im), and realIF promotes it to an IntermediateField ℚ ℂ. Because the single generator a is real, adjoin_le_iff gives ℚ(⁴√2) ≤ realIF. The crux I_not_mem_adjoin_a then follows in one line: if i ∈ ℚ(⁴√2) ≤ realIF then Im(i) = 0, contradicting Im(i) = 1. This is exactly what makes the closure proper (degree 8, not 4).
mathContext: A real subfield of ℂ cannot contain i; packaging ℝ as an intermediate field turns this into ℚ(⁴√2) ≤ realIF ∌ i.

title: Adjoining i: the degree-2 second step
content: i is integral over ℚ(⁴√2), a root of the monic X² + 1 (I_isIntegral). To pin its minimal polynomial, X2_add_one_no_root shows X² + 1 has no root in ℚ(⁴√2): a root x would satisfy x² = −1, but every element of ℚ(⁴√2) is real (via realIF), and a real number's square is nonnegative. A degree-2 polynomial over a field with no root is irreducible (irreducible_of_degree_le_three_of_not_isRoot), so minpoly_I gives minpoly = X² + 1 and finrank_step_two gives [ℚ(⁴√2, i):ℚ(⁴√2)] = 2.
mathContext: The strict top step of the tower comes from irreducibility of X² + 1 over the real base field.

title: The tower law: [ℚ(⁴√2, i) : ℚ] = 8
content: With both steps in hand, the tower law Module.finrank_mul_finrank multiplies them: finrank_tower gives [ℚ(⁴√2)(i):ℚ] = [ℚ(⁴√2):ℚ]·[ℚ(⁴√2, i):ℚ(⁴√2)] = 4·2 = 8 (an explicit FiniteDimensional instance and a raised synthInstance budget are needed for the tower's typeclass search). galois_closure_eq_adjoin_pair uses adjoin_simple_adjoin_simple to identify the two-step ℚ(⁴√2)(i) with the pair adjunction ℚ(⁴√2, i), so finrank_galois_closure states the headline: [ℚ(⁴√2, i):ℚ] = 8.
mathContext: 8 = |D₄| is the order of the Galois group; the degree computation secures it without naming the group.

title: The four roots and the splitting-field property
content: Finally the entry certifies that ℚ(⁴√2, i) really is the splitting field. I_mul_a_pow_four shows the non-real root i·⁴√2 satisfies (i·⁴√2)⁴ = 2 (since i⁴ = 1), and roots_mem_closure shows all four roots ±⁴√2, ±i·⁴√2 lie in ℚ(⁴√2, i) (from a, i ∈ the closure and closure under negation and product). So X⁴ − 2 splits over ℚ(⁴√2, i), the defining property of the splitting field.
mathContext: The four roots form a square in ℂ; the Galois group D₄ is its symmetry group.
prerequisites: closure of a field under negation and multiplication
